rewrites.summary:
A visitor to this region stands under the national framework in force across the autonomous communities: the 2023 national trans-equality law allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration without prior medical diagnosis or treatment and provides for corresponding document adaptation, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2 July 2005, so marriage and partner-travel carry full legal effect. The law also prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing and enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples.

Practical safety is comparatively favourable on the record: no region-specific adverse incident, ordinance or enforcement finding was identified for this region in the country dossier, no sub-national facility, expression or assembly restriction exists anywhere in the country, and the region contains one of the country's densest, most visible LGBTI urban centres with dedicated hate-crime structures within its own regional police force. The national victimisation baseline nonetheless applies — a 2026 federation report found 44% of LGBTI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident — with the dossier's fault line being city-versus-rural rather than region-versus-region.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The national reform's implementation, including its education-facing parts, falls to the regional government, so local enforcement posture rather than statute carries the residual variation in what a visitor experiences. The region holds front-runner status inside the country's framework — its 1998 couples law was the first Spanish couples law extending minimum legal provisions to homosexual couples, and its 2014 autonomous statute prompted the 2010s wave of regional LGBTI laws — a comparison within the parent state rather than a separate risk. A 2023 provision permitting recognition for children from age 12 under conditions proved contentious, and the international rights organisation Human Rights Watch placed the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing instruments: the autonomous statute of 10 October 2014 defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, obliges the regional public administrations to ensure administrative documentation reflects gender identity, extends protections across education, health, employment and sport, and guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects; an independent oversight body can instigate proceedings, and minor breaches carry fines between seven days' and three months' worth of the regional income-sufficiency indicator.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No region-specific adverse incident, ordinance or enforcement finding was identified in the country dossier for this region, so the assessment rests on the national framework and the national victimisation survey rather than regional enforcement data. No region-specific border-screening or visitor-document practice is recorded in the dossier; the registry-based document adaptation is national, and marriage and partner-travel relevance rests on the national same-sex marriage position. Whether the 44% baseline translates into region-specific incident rates is unverifiable from the sourced claims.

blindSourceSummaries: Official gazette text of the national trans-equality law of 28 February 2023, applying uniformly across the autonomous communities: adults may rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, with corresponding document adaptation and mandated public-policy, workplace, health and education measures.

rewrites.summary:
This division is assessed at the national score: the dedicated country dossier that covered it identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (within ±0.02), so a visitor stands under the national pattern. A 2025 national feature described the trans community facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation', with the national anti-discrimination agency closed, the national ministry responsible for gender and diversity portfolios eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota dismissed.

Practical safety for a traveler is set by the national profile: a 2026 report from a national hate-crime observatory counted at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — up 62% year on year, its highest count in ten years, one every 38 hours, with trans women and travestis 62.5% of victims — and tied the surge to institutional weakening and government legitimation of discriminatory discourse; this province sits under that pattern with no separate local record.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National-policy turbulence: the 2025 feature attributes the worsening situation to the national administration's direction — closure of the national anti-discrimination agency and elimination of the dedicated national ministry — rather than to provincial action, and the observatory tied the 2025 rise in hate crimes to institutional weakening and government legitimation of discriminatory discourse. No litigation flux or comparison with neighbouring divisions is documented in the dossier for this province.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data: the labour-inclusion quota hires are a public-sector employment rule for local trans residents, with 2024 dismissals under the national administration; the hate-crime tallies count local residents as victims and so are resident violence data rather than a visitor incident series. No province-specific resident discrimination data beyond the national pattern is recorded in the dossier.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The assessment rests on the country dossier's no-material-deviation finding bounded by the ±0.02 threshold, and the sources are national reports without separate local reporting for this province. No provincial border-screening or visitor-document practice is recorded in the dossier, and no division-specific enforcement series or incident data beyond the national tallies is on file; a national baseline is not proof of province-level practice either way.
